sections.h2: Who sends and who values your Franklin County bill
sections.html:
Two Franklin County offices touch your bill. The Tax Commissioner bills and collects. The Board of Tax Assessors appraises property and approves exemptions. Neither one sets the rate: the county commissioners and the school board do that.

The money pays for county government and the public schools, courts, the jail and law enforcement, county roads and fire protection, public buildings and bridges, and public health and sanitation.

The Tax Commissioner is at 1221 Hull Avenue in Carnesville, the county seat. Mail goes to PO Box 100, Carnesville, GA 30521, and the phone is 706-384-3455. For questions about value, exemptions or returns, call the Tax Assessor at 706-384-4896.

sections.h2: How the amount you owe is calculated
sections.html:
The assessed value is 40 percent of the house's market value. Exemptions come off that figure, and the millage rate is applied to what remains. A mill is $1 for each $1,000. Your bill shows both numbers, so you can check the math line by line.

A buyer, or any owner who changed the property, files form PT-50r with the assessor between January 1 and April 1. Skipping it costs 10 percent of the omitted value plus interest. If nothing changed from last year, no return is needed.

sections.h2: Franklin County tax dates and rates
sections.html:
Franklin County property tax basics
Event or chargeDate or amount
Bills dueNormally November 15
Interest after the due date1 percent per month
Added penalty10 percent, if still unpaid at day 90
Assessment appeal window45 days after the notice
Homestead and return filingJanuary 1 to April 1
Mobile home return and permitOn or before May 1
Tax salesA first Tuesday, at the courthouse

Homesteaded property owing under $500 is spared the 10 percent penalty.

After November 15 the clock starts. Interest runs at 1 percent a month, and the 10 percent surcharge lands at 90 days. The county then files a fifa, or execution, with the Clerk of Superior Court. Anyone can read it, and credit bureaus may pull it. The tax office has no say over how they use it.

Only full payment of the delinquent taxes releases the lien. If the taxes stay unpaid, the tax commissioner, who also serves as ex-officio sheriff, can levy on the property and auction it. The office calls that a last resort.

If a bill is open when you sell, call 706-384-3455 and ask for the amount owed through your closing date. Give that number to your closing agent so the payoff comes out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: Where does a value dispute go?
sections.html:
The notice carries a date, and your 45 days count from it. The assessors review the value again and send you a decision. If they stand by their number, the Board of Equalization hears the dispute next. After that, Superior Court is open on written notice to the assessors.

Arbitration can replace the equalization hearing. You can raise taxability, value, or uniformity among comparable parcels. You cannot appeal the tax rate itself, since other bodies set it.

Before you file, pull your parcel record and gather recent sales of similar homes nearby. Photos of damage or needed repairs help too.

sections.h2: Exemptions that lower a Franklin County bill
sections.html:
One application with the Tax Assessor starts the exemption, and it renews each year until the owner changes or asks for a different type. Ownership and occupancy count as of January 1. April 1 is the filing deadline. File early and have the assessor confirm the date for your year.

  • Standard homestead: $2,000 subtracted from assessed value.
  • Age 65 and older, local exemption: $20,000 against all taxes on the homestead.
  • Age 62 and older, floating exemption: tied to natural increases in value, with an income cap of $30,000.
  • A disabled veteran: $100,896, which a surviving spouse who has not remarried, or minor children, can keep.
  • Deferral program: for homeowners aged 62 or over earning no more than $15,000 gross, payment can wait until the property changes hands or the deferred balance and interest climb to 85 percent of its value.

The assessors make the final call on eligibility. A denied applicant gets notice and an appeal path.

Qualifying farm property can be assessed at 30 percent rather than 40. Under conservation use, farm and timber land is valued at its current use instead of market value, but the owner signs a covenant to keep it in that use for ten years. File with the assessors by April 1 and pay a $25 recording fee.

Breaking the covenant costs twice the taxes saved. There is no penalty after a death or a condemnation, and one year of savings is owed after a medically shown illness or a foreclosure. A sale does not trigger the penalty when the buyer signs the covenant and keeps the same use.

Standing timber is untaxed until it is cut or sold, then it is valued at 100 percent of market. A mobile or modular home is taxed as personal property each year. Its return and location permit are due by May 1, and the year's tax must be paid first.

sections.h2: Other things the tax office handles
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner also runs the county tag office in the Court House Annex at 1221 Hull Avenue, open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. Renew a tag in the 30 days leading up to the owner's birthday. A vehicle you just bought must be registered within 30 days. Some private websites charge extra for renewals, so use the Georgia Department of Revenue site.

Tax paid in error can be refunded on a written claim to the board of commissioners made within three years. Refunds rest on errors. A disagreement over value goes through the appeal process instead. Owners of personal property file a PT-50p return every year by April 1, whether or not anything changed.

Older materials may mention a Homeowner's Tax Relief Grant. The state stopped funding that credit after the 2009 tax year, so you will not see it on a current bill.

Auctions are held on a first Tuesday outside the courthouse. The county advertises each sale in the Franklin County Citizen every week for a month beforehand. Bidding starts at what the parcel owes in taxes, fees and interest.

Redemption stays open for twelve months. The owner, a creditor or another party with an interest can redeem. The price is the buyer's purchase amount, any taxes the buyer paid since, special assessments, and a premium: 20 percent for the first year or portion, then 10 percent for each added year or portion. During that time the buyer cannot take possession, collect rent or improve the property. Take foreclosure questions to an attorney.

Franklin County has 25,948 people, up 10.8 percent since April 2020. It holds 11,475 housing units, and owners occupy 77.2 percent of the lived-in ones. The median owner-occupied home is worth $179,000. About 19.6 percent of residents are 65 or older, so the senior exemptions above reach a sizable share of owners.

Before you list, check that your parcel shows no open bill, and confirm which exemptions are on file. A buyer's title search will turn up any execution on record, so clearing one early keeps the closing on schedule. If taxes are owed, a cash sale that closes quickly can pay the balance out of the proceeds and skip the added months of interest.

faqs.q: When must Franklin County taxes be paid?
faqs.a: By November 15 in the usual case. Late bills add 1 percent interest a month, plus a 10 percent penalty at the 90-day mark.

faqs.q: Who explains my Franklin County property value?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessor, 706-384-4896. The Tax Commissioner, 706-384-3455, handles billing and payment only.

faqs.q: How long do Franklin County owners have to contest a value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the notice's date. Start with the assessors; the equalization board or arbitration is next, and Superior Court is last.

faqs.q: Does Franklin County give older homeowners a break?
faqs.a: Yes. There is a local $20,000 exemption for homeowners 65 and older, separate state breaks at ages 62 and 65 with income limits, and a deferral option with a $15,000 gross income ceiling.

faqs.q: Can an owner redeem after a Franklin County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, for twelve months, by paying the buyer the itemized redemption amount, which carries a 20 percent premium in year one. The tax deed holder gets no possession during that year.
